title: Jason Calacanis on angel investing, founder traits, and building a syndicate
summary: Jason explains how he picks founders (broken, driven, with something to prove), why startups are war and sports, and how radical delegation and a syndicate let him invest at scale. He also covers product-market fit, compounding, riding winners, and deal terms.

principles.text: Product-market fit is fixed by improving the product, not the packaging.
principles.quote: instead of making the burger better, they do everything but the burger. So, they change the furniture in the restaurant. They changed the name of the store

principles.text: Make ten things 10% better rather than one thing twice as good.
principles.quote: it's very hard to make one feature of your product twice as good, but it's very easy to make 10 of your features 10% better.

principles.text: Look at the upside case first; red flags are a roadmap of what to fix, not a reason to pass.
principles.quote: I say make a list of all the things that could go wrong. And then on the other side of your journal, list the things, you know, but what if it goes right, but what if it works?

principles.text: Radically delegate and spend time only on the highest-leverage activities.
principles.quote: I am ruthless about delegation. Uh and I get more ruthless.

principles.text: Ride your winners and avoid selling too early; the last doublings are the most valuable.
principles.quote: if you get $10 million in an exit and you sell your Facebook shares for 10 million bucks, if you had held them, you would have had another 10x.

principles.text: Standard clean deal terms keep the cap table aligned; funky terms scare off later investors.
principles.quote: We don't do funky stuff like that because it's against our best interest in the long term
